menopause.name: Menopause and perimenopause
menopause.definition: Menopause is when periods stop altogether, and perimenopause is the stage before this when periods change and symptoms begin.
menopause.overview: Perimenopause is the time when someone has symptoms of the menopause but their periods have not yet stopped. Menopause is when periods stop altogether. The NHS says menopause usually affects women between the ages of 45 and 55, but it can happen earlier. Symptoms can start months or years before periods stop, and some, such as joint pain and vaginal dryness, can continue afterwards. Hormone replacement therapy is the main treatment, and other options exist for people who cannot or do not want to use it.
causes: The ovaries make less of the hormone oestrogen and no longer release an egg each month.
Surgery to remove both ovaries causes menopause straight away.
Chemotherapy or radiotherapy can affect the ovaries and bring on menopause.
For many people who have an early menopause, no cause can be found.
riskFactors: A family history of early menopause is linked with a higher chance of it.
Starting periods early is linked with early menopause.
Smoking is linked with early menopause.
Being underweight is linked with early menopause.
signs: Periods that become irregular or less frequent, which is often the first sign of perimenopause.
Vaginal dryness, which can continue after periods stop.
complications: Early menopause raises the chance of bone and heart problems.
Major bone loss in women happens with the loss of oestrogen at the menopause.
menopause.diagnosis: The NHS says menopause is usually diagnosed in women over 45. For early menopause, a GP may use symptoms, family history and blood tests to check hormone levels.
menopause.treatment: Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is the main treatment for menopause and perimenopause symptoms. If HRT is unsuitable or not wanted, options include cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), and a doctor may suggest clonidine or an antidepressant. Herbal remedies and compounded bioidentical hormones are not recommended for menopause symptoms, according to NHS guidance.
menopause.prevention: Natural menopause is a change linked to ageing, so it is not something that can be prevented. Women's Health Concern lists exercise, sunshine and a balanced diet as the basis for bone health.
menopause.seekCare: The NHS advises contacting a GP for anyone who thinks they have symptoms and wants to know the options. It also advises contacting a GP about any vaginal bleeding after a year without a period.

sections.heading: What are perimenopause and menopause?
sections.body:
Perimenopause is the time when someone has symptoms of the menopause but their periods have not stopped. Menopause is when periods stop altogether. The NHS says periods usually become less frequent over a few months or years before they stop altogether. For some people, periods can stop suddenly. Perimenopause can last from months to years. The NHS also says someone reaches menopause once they have not had a period for 12 months.

NHS inform Scotland describes menopause as a change in hormone balance linked to ageing. It says the ovaries make less of the hormone oestrogen and no longer release an egg each month. The NHS says menopause usually affects women between the ages of 45 and 55, but it can happen earlier. Early menopause can follow surgery to remove the ovaries or cancer treatment. The NHS describes the first sign of perimenopause as often being irregular periods, which may come more or less often and be heavier or lighter than before.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms?
sections.body:
A change in the usual pattern of periods is often the first sign of perimenopause. For example, periods may become irregular. The NHS lists mood changes such as low mood, anxiety and low self-esteem among the common symptoms. It also lists poor memory and problems with concentration.

Physical symptoms include hot flushes, sleep problems, palpitations, and headaches or migraines that are worse than usual. Muscle aches and joint pains, skin changes and reduced sex drive are also listed. Joint pain and vaginal dryness can continue after periods stop. Symptoms can last for months or years, and they can change over time. Women's Health Concern says that sleep problems are very common in the menopause transition. Vaginal dryness can also make sex uncomfortable for some women, according to NHS inform Scotland. Bleeding after sex can also be a sign of a health condition, and NHS inform Scotland advises contacting a GP about it.

sections.heading: How are they diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says menopause is usually diagnosed in women over 45. The NHS advises contacting a GP for anyone who thinks they have symptoms of menopause or perimenopause and wants to know the options. It says early advice can help reduce the effects on health, relationships and work.

For early menopause, a GP may use symptoms, family history and blood tests to check hormone levels. The NHS also advises contacting a GP about palpitations, or if bleeding has changed so that it is heavier than before. Bleeding after the menopause needs to be checked by a GP, even if it happens once or is only spotting. Bleeding of this kind can be due to thinning of the womb lining, and less often to womb cancer. NICE updated its menopause guideline in 2024 and says it clarified when to refer people to a healthcare professional with expertise in menopause, fertility, or both.

sections.heading: What is hormone replacement therapy?
sections.body:
Hormone replacement therapy, or HRT, is the main treatment for menopause and perimenopause symptoms. The NHS describes it as an effective treatment for most people going through menopause and perimenopause. It also says HRT can help prevent thinning of the bones, which can lead to fracture (osteoporosis). For people under 60 who have symptoms and are not at high risk of breast cancer or blood clots, the NHS says the benefits are likely to outweigh the risks.

NHS 111 Wales says combined HRT, which contains oestrogen and progestogen, is associated with a small increased risk of breast cancer. NHS guidance says this risk rises the longer HRT is taken and falls after it is stopped. The Wales page says the breast cancer risk is linked to all types of HRT except vaginal oestrogen. The NHS says HRT tablets can increase the risk of blood clots, although the risk is very low. It says patches or gels carry no increased risk of blood clots. The NHS says the decision depends on age, symptoms and personal risk factors.

sections.heading: What other treatments and self-care are described?
sections.body:
If HRT does not work, cannot be taken or is not wanted, the NHS says other types of treatment are available. These include cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). NICE added menopause-specific CBT in its 2024 update of guideline NG23. It says this can be considered for hot flushes and night sweats, including alongside HRT or when someone prefers not to take HRT. Clonidine is a prescription medicine that can help reduce hot flushes and night sweats. Antidepressants are used for mood symptoms in people diagnosed with depression or anxiety.

Fezolinetant is a non-hormonal medicine taken by mouth for moderate to severe hot flushes and night sweats. MedlinePlus says it blocks a brain chemical called neurokinin B from binding to its receptors in the hypothalamus. NICE guidance covers its use when HRT is unsuitable. Herbal remedies such as red clover and black cohosh have no strong evidence that they work, according to the NHS. Women's Health Concern describes weight-bearing exercise as any exercise on the feet or legs that works against gravity. It stresses regular activity for bone health and lists exercise, sunshine and a balanced diet as the basis of bone health.

sections.heading: What is early or premature menopause?
sections.body:
Early menopause is when regular periods stop before the age of 45. Premature menopause is when this happens before the age of 40, and it is also called premature ovarian insufficiency. It can be natural or be caused by treatment, such as radiotherapy or surgery to remove the ovaries. For most people, no cause can be found.

Early menopause raises the chance of bone and heart problems. The NHS says it is important to replace the missing hormones when menopause starts before 45. The main treatments are the combined contraceptive pill or HRT, and lifestyle changes can also help. Fertility may be affected. The British Menopause Society advises that bone density assessment should be considered when premature ovarian insufficiency is diagnosed. It also says HRT may improve bone health and heart markers more than the combined oral contraceptive pill.

faqs.q: At what age does menopause usually happen?
faqs.a: The NHS says menopause usually affects women between the ages of 45 and 55, but it can happen earlier. Periods usually become less frequent over a few months or years before they stop altogether. For some people, periods can stop suddenly. Early menopause is when periods stop before the age of 45.

faqs.q: Is HRT the only treatment for menopause symptoms?
faqs.a: HRT is the main treatment, but it is not the only one. If it is unsuitable or not wanted, the NHS says other treatments are available. These include cognitive behavioural therapy, and a doctor may suggest clonidine or an antidepressant. Herbal remedies and compounded bioidentical hormones are not recommended, according to NHS guidance.

faqs.q: How is menopause diagnosed?
faqs.a: The NHS says menopause is usually diagnosed in women over 45. For early menopause, a GP may use symptoms, family history and blood tests to check hormone levels. The NHS advises contacting a GP for anyone who thinks they have symptoms and wants to know the options. It says early advice can help reduce the effects on health, relationships and work.

faqs.q: Can symptoms carry on after periods stop?
faqs.a: Yes, some symptoms can. The NHS says joint pain and vaginal dryness can continue after periods stop. Symptoms can last for months or years, and they can change over time. A GP appointment is the route to discuss the options.

faqs.q: When should someone see a GP about menopause?
faqs.a: The NHS advises contacting a GP for anyone who thinks they have symptoms of perimenopause or menopause and wants to know the options. The NHS also advises contacting a GP about any vaginal bleeding after a year without a period. It also advises contacting a GP about palpitations. Early advice can help reduce the effects on health, relationships and work.

erectile-dysfunction.name: Erectile dysfunction
erectile-dysfunction.definition: Erectile dysfunction, also called impotence, is being unable to get or keep an erection.
erectile-dysfunction.overview: Erectile dysfunction, also called impotence, means being unable to get or keep an erection. Occasional problems are common and are often linked to stress, tiredness or heavy drinking. When the problem keeps happening, the NHS says it might be a sign of a health condition that can be treated, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol or hormone problems. Treatment includes medicines called PDE-5 inhibitors, counselling and treatment of any underlying condition.

Some medicines, as a side effect
High blood pressure or high cholesterol
Diabetes
Anxiety
Hormone problems
Psychological factors such as performance pressure, anxiety or feelings about the partner or relationship
riskFactors: Long-term conditions such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes
Heavy drinking
Taking a medicine that can cause erection problems as a side effect
complications: It can be one of the first warning signs of atherosclerosis, according to the British Heart Foundation
erectile-dysfunction.diagnosis: At an appointment, the doctor or nurse may ask about lifestyle and relationships, discuss any problems, carry out some health checks and examine the genitals to rule out physical causes.
erectile-dysfunction.treatment: The NHS says the main treatments are medicines called PDE-5 inhibitors, which increase blood flow to the penis. Underlying conditions can also be treated. Counselling can help when emotional or mental health factors are involved. Vacuum pumps can be used when medicine is not suitable or does not work, though they are not always available on the NHS.
erectile-dysfunction.prevention: The NHS lists stopping smoking, eating a healthy diet and exercising as lifestyle changes that can help.
erectile-dysfunction.seekCare: For erection problems that keep happening, a routine appointment with a GP or a visit to a sexual health clinic is the route the NHS names. NHS inform says to contact the GP practice if symptoms have lasted more than a few months, self-help has not worked and the person is bothered by them. A painful erection that lasts a long time needs care at A&E according to the NHS, and NHS 111 Wales says to call 999 or go to A&E.

sections.heading: What is erectile dysfunction?
sections.body: The NHS describes erectile dysfunction, also called impotence, as being unable to get or keep an erection. The NHS says that occasional problems with erections are common. Occasional problems are often linked to stress, tiredness or heavy drinking, according to the NHS. When the problem keeps happening, the NHS says it might be a sign of a health condition that can be treated. High blood pressure, high cholesterol and hormone problems are among the conditions the NHS links to it, and the Sexual Advice Association says erection problems can be associated with diabetes. The NHS says a GP or a sexual health clinic is the place to go when erection problems keep happening, and that sexual health clinics can offer the same treatment as a GP. NHS inform adds that people are advised to contact their GP practice when symptoms have lasted more than a few months, self-help has not worked and the problem is bothering them.

sections.heading: What can cause erection problems?
sections.body: The NHS says some medicines can cause erection problems as a side effect. Long-term conditions can also play a part, including high blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes, and the NHS mentions hormone problems as another cause. The British Heart Foundation notes that stress, anxiety or excessive alcohol can contribute, and that some heart medicines can too. Heavy drinking is one of the everyday reasons the NHS gives for occasional problems. The Sexual Advice Association explains that erection problems that only happen with a partner can still have a physical cause. For that reason, it says a check with a GP comes first. If the physical checks come back clear, it says psychological causes may be involved. It gives performance pressure, anxiety and feelings about the partner or relationship as examples, and also lists a traumatic experience, attraction issues and a fear of climaxing with someone else.

sections.heading: Can erectile dysfunction be a sign of heart disease?
sections.body: The Sexual Advice Association says erection problems can be an early sign of heart disease. It also says they can be associated with diabetes. The British Heart Foundation explains that during an erection the arteries to the penis widen to let more blood flow in. If arteries in the body are affected by atherosclerosis, blood flow is reduced, including to the penis. The charity notes that because the arteries of the penis are so narrow, erection problems can be one of the first warning signs. MedlinePlus, a US health resource, also describes erectile dysfunction as a flag for a higher risk of atherosclerosis and its complications. It says that in its early stages atherosclerosis often does not cause any symptoms. For these reasons, the Sexual Advice Association says a thorough check by a GP matters. The British Heart Foundation also notes that some heart medicines can contribute to erection problems.

sections.heading: How is erectile dysfunction diagnosed?
sections.body: The NHS says that at an appointment the doctor or nurse may ask about lifestyle and relationships, discuss any problems, carry out some health checks and examine the genitals to rule out physical causes. The Sexual Advice Association says a GP check is the first step, so that physical causes can be looked for. If the physical checks come back clear, it says psychological causes may be involved. The NHS says a GP or a sexual health clinic is the place to go when erection problems keep happening. It says sexual health clinics can offer the same treatment as a GP, and that many have a walk-in service where an appointment is not needed. The NHS also says a doctor may switch a person to a different medicine if the medicine they take is causing the erection problem. Treatment for erection problems is described in the next section.

sections.heading: How is erectile dysfunction treated?
sections.body: The NHS says the main treatments are medicines called PDE-5 inhibitors, which increase blood flow to the penis. The NHS names sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil and avanafil as examples. A NICE evidence summary says that first-line treatment is usually an oral PDE-5 inhibitor. The NHS says sildenafil can be bought from a pharmacy after a conversation with the pharmacist, who checks general health and may refer the person to a doctor. It warns that medicines sold online are not always regulated and that ingredients can vary, so they may cause unpleasant side effects or may not be suitable. Treating an underlying condition is another approach. Counselling can help when emotional or mental health factors are involved, though the NHS says there can be a long wait for these services on the NHS. Vacuum pumps can be used when medicine is not suitable or does not work, though they are not always available on the NHS.

sections.heading: What helps with talking and everyday life?
sections.body: The NHS lists lifestyle changes that can help, including stopping smoking, eating a healthy diet and exercising. It also lists losing weight for people who are overweight, and NHS 111 Wales mentions reducing stress and anxiety. The Sexual Advice Association suggests telling a partner that things need to go slowly, and focusing on kissing and cuddling rather than on getting an erection. It describes sex therapy as a talking therapy in which an individual or couple works with an experienced therapist to assess and treat sexual or relationship problems. It says a GP or another NHS health professional may be able to refer someone for sex therapy, depending on the area. Sex therapy can also be arranged by contacting a therapist directly and paying privately. If problems continue, it suggests a sex therapist.

sections.heading: When is it an emergency?
sections.body: A painful erection that lasts a long time is called priapism. The NHS says a prolonged erection needs care at A&E because of the risk of permanent damage. NHS 111 Wales says a person with this problem should not drive themselves, and that someone else can drive or 999 can be called. Hospital trust leaflets describe sickle cell disease as the most common cause of priapism. They say that, if it is not treated, priapism can lead to scarring and a lasting inability to get an erection. They also say hospital treatment can include draining blood from the penis with a needle, medicines and, sometimes, surgery. NHS 111 Wales gives a shorter time limit than the NHS priapism page, so the length of time that counts as an emergency differs between sources. Ordinary erection problems that keep happening are different, and the NHS says a GP or sexual health clinic is the place to start.

faqs.q: Is erectile dysfunction common?
faqs.a: The NHS says that occasional problems with erections are common. Occasional problems are often linked to stress, tiredness or heavy drinking, according to the NHS. When the problem keeps happening, the NHS says it might be a sign of a health condition that can be treated, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol or hormone problems. The NHS says a GP or a sexual health clinic is the place to go when erection problems keep happening.

faqs.q: Can erectile dysfunction be a sign of another health problem?
faqs.a: The NHS says persistent erection problems might be a sign of a health condition that can be treated, and it links high blood pressure, high cholesterol and hormone problems to them. The Sexual Advice Association says erection problems can be an early sign of heart disease and can be associated with diabetes. The British Heart Foundation says they can be one of the first warning signs of atherosclerosis. The Sexual Advice Association says a thorough check by a GP matters for this reason.

faqs.q: What treatments are there?
faqs.a: The NHS says the main treatments are medicines called PDE-5 inhibitors, which increase blood flow to the penis. The NHS also names counselling, treatment of underlying conditions and vacuum pumps. Which options are available on the NHS can vary, and the NHS says vacuum pumps are not always available on the NHS. Counselling services can have a long wait on the NHS.

faqs.q: Can worry or stress cause it?
faqs.a: The NHS links occasional problems to stress, tiredness and heavy drinking. The Sexual Advice Association lists performance pressure, anxiety and feelings about the partner or relationship as psychological causes. It says these are considered once a GP has checked for physical causes. Counselling can help when emotional or mental health factors are involved.

enlarged-prostate.name: Enlarged prostate (benign prostatic hyperplasia)
enlarged-prostate.definition: An enlarged prostate is a common condition in which the prostate gland grows larger and can squeeze the urethra, the outlet tube for urine, slowing the flow of urine from the bladder.
enlarged-prostate.overview: An enlarged prostate, also called benign prostate enlargement, is common and is not usually serious, according to the NHS. It is most common in men over 50. The main symptoms are problems with peeing, such as difficulty starting, a weak flow and needing to pee more often. Treatments can help for men who need them, and the NHS says an enlarged prostate is not linked to a higher risk of prostate cancer.
causes: Changes in hormone levels as a man gets older, which the NHS links with the condition
riskFactors: Being over 50, when the condition is most common
complications: Acute urinary retention, the sudden inability to pass any urine, which is painful and treated as an emergency
Urinary tract infection, and later urine retention, bladder stones, bladder infections and kidney damage
enlarged-prostate.diagnosis: The NHS says a GP may start with a questionnaire about the symptoms and will want to rule out other conditions that cause similar symptoms. A urine sample may be tested, a PSA blood test may be considered, and a rectal examination lets the doctor feel the size and shape of the prostate. The GP may also ask for a diary of what is drunk and how much pee is passed.
enlarged-prostate.treatment: The NHS says treatment depends on how much the symptoms affect daily life. For mild symptoms, lifestyle changes usually come first. Medicines include alpha blockers, which relax muscles around the bladder and prostate and can make it easier to pee, and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, which shrink the prostate. Surgery is usually only recommended for moderate to severe symptoms that have not responded to medication.
enlarged-prostate.prevention: The NHS describes lifestyle measures that can ease symptoms. These include cutting down on alcohol and caffeine, keeping to a healthy weight and avoiding constipation.
enlarged-prostate.seekCare: Suddenly being unable to pass any urine is an emergency: NHS inform describes acute urinary retention as a medical emergency, and MyHealth Devon advises going immediately to the nearest A&E. The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111 for blood in the pee or pain when peeing. For other urinary symptoms, a GP can carry out the assessment, which may include a questionnaire, urine and PSA tests and a rectal examination.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of an enlarged prostate?
sections.body:
The NHS describes the main symptoms of an enlarged prostate as problems with peeing. These include difficulty starting to pee, straining, a weak flow, a feeling that the bladder has not emptied fully, dribbling, and needing to pee more often or urgently, including at night. The symptoms usually develop slowly and may gradually get worse as a man gets older.

NHS information leaflets note that the severity of symptoms is not always related to the size of the prostate, so a larger gland does not always mean worse symptoms. The prostate sits around the urethra, and as it grows it can squeeze that outlet tube and slow the flow of urine from the bladder. NHS inform adds that, later on, the condition can cause urine retention and other complications such as bladder stones, bladder infections and kidney damage.

sections.heading: What causes an enlarged prostate?
sections.body:
The NHS links benign prostate enlargement to changes in hormone levels as a man gets older, and it is most common in men over 50. The NHS describes the condition as common and not usually serious, although there are treatments that can help if they are needed.

The prostate sits around the urethra. As the prostate grows, it starts to squeeze this outlet tube, which slows the flow of urine from the bladder. Over time this can lead to problems such as acute urinary retention, which is described further below.

Many men worry that an enlarged prostate means a higher risk of prostate cancer. The NHS says an enlarged prostate is not linked to a higher risk of prostate cancer, and a clinical director at NHS England has made the same point, saying that many men worry about this but it is not the case. When the symptoms are assessed, the GP will also want to rule out other conditions that cause similar symptoms.

sections.heading: How is an enlarged prostate diagnosed?
sections.body:
According to the NHS, a GP may start with a questionnaire that assesses the symptoms, and will want to rule out other conditions that cause similar symptoms. Tests can include a rectal examination, in which the doctor feels the size and shape of the prostate through a gloved finger in the back passage. A urine sample may be tested for problems, and the GP may ask for a diary of how much is drunk and how much pee is passed.

A PSA blood test may also be considered. NHS information says it gives a rough idea of how large the prostate may be and how quickly it is growing, and that a high result does not mean cancer. NHS inform says a PSA test cannot give a definite diagnosis of prostate cancer. If further tests are needed, a specialist called a urologist may carry them out.

sections.heading: How is an enlarged prostate treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says treatment depends on how much the symptoms affect daily life. For mild symptoms, lifestyle changes usually come first. These include cutting down on alcohol and caffeine, keeping to a healthy weight and avoiding constipation. MyHealth Devon also lists eating more fibre, because constipation can add pressure on the bladder.

Medicines include alpha blockers, such as tamsulosin and alfuzosin, which relax the muscles around the bladder and prostate and can make it easier to pee. Finasteride and dutasteride are 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, which shrink the prostate gland. NHS inform says that for moderate to severe symptoms, medication is usually recommended as well as lifestyle changes.

Surgery is usually only recommended for moderate to severe symptoms that have not responded to medication. The most common operation is transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), which removes part of the prostate through a thin tube passed up the penis. Another option is HoLEP, which uses a laser. Newer minimally invasive options, including Rezum steam therapy and UroLift implants, have also been offered in England.

sections.heading: When should you get medical help?
sections.body:
Acute urinary retention is the sudden inability to pass any urine. NHS inform says it should be treated as a medical emergency, because without prompt treatment urine may be passed back up into the kidneys, which can damage them. MyHealth Devon lists its warning signs as suddenly not being able to pee at all, severe lower tummy pain and a swollen bladder that can be felt, and advises going immediately to the nearest A&E. Treatment is usually with a urinary catheter, according to MyHealth Devon.

For blood in the pee or pain when peeing, the NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111.

NHS inform says benign prostate enlargement can sometimes lead to complications such as a urinary tract infection or acute urinary retention. A GP is the usual first contact for other urinary symptoms, and the assessment is described in the diagnosis section above.

faqs.q: Does an enlarged prostate mean prostate cancer?
faqs.a: The NHS says an enlarged prostate is not linked to a higher risk of prostate cancer. A clinical director at NHS England has said that many men worry it is, but this is not the case. When urinary symptoms are assessed, the GP will also want to rule out other conditions that cause similar symptoms, and the NHS notes that a high PSA result does not mean cancer.

faqs.q: Does an enlarged prostate always need treatment?
faqs.a: The NHS says treatment depends on how much the symptoms affect daily life. For mild symptoms, lifestyle changes usually come first. NHS inform says medication is usually recommended alongside lifestyle changes for moderate to severe symptoms, and that surgery is usually only recommended when symptoms are moderate to severe and have not responded to medication.

faqs.q: Is BPH the same as an enlarged prostate?
faqs.a: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a name used on NHS pages for the same condition that other NHS pages call an enlarged prostate or benign prostate enlargement. In each case the prostate grows larger and can squeeze the urethra, slowing the flow of urine. The NHS says it is common, not usually serious, and most common in men over 50.

faqs.q: What happens if a man cannot pass urine?
faqs.a: Suddenly being unable to pass any urine is called acute urinary retention. NHS inform says it should be treated as a medical emergency, because urine can pass back up towards the kidneys and damage them. MyHealth Devon advises going immediately to the nearest A&E, and says treatment is usually with a urinary catheter.

faqs.q: Can lifestyle changes help with an enlarged prostate?
faqs.a: The NHS says that for mild symptoms lifestyle changes usually come first. The measures it lists include cutting down on alcohol and caffeine, keeping to a healthy weight and avoiding constipation. MyHealth Devon also lists eating more fibre. For moderate to severe symptoms, NHS inform says medication is usually recommended as well as lifestyle changes.

gonorrhoea.name: Gonorrhoea
gonorrhoea.definition: A bacterial sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae that can affect the genitals, rectum, throat and eyes.
gonorrhoea.overview: Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by a bacterium called Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It can affect the genitals, rectum, throat and eyes. Not everyone has symptoms, so testing matters when infection is possible. In England, UKHSA reports that around half of diagnoses are in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men. Treatment is with antibiotics, and if it is given early, lasting problems are unlikely.
causes: Infection with the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Passed on through vaginal, anal or oral sex without a condom, or contact with infected secretions
Sharing sex toys that have not been washed or covered with a new condom each time
Passed from a mother to her baby during birth
People without symptoms can still pass it on
riskFactors: Sex without a condom or other barrier
Previous infection, which gives no lasting protection against catching it again
In England, being a gay, bisexual or other man who has sex with men, as this group accounts for around half of diagnoses
signs: Discharge from the penis, or a change in vaginal discharge
Red, itchy or painful eyes when the eyes are infected
complications: Pelvic inflammatory disease in women, which can lead to long-term pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy and infertility
Painful infection of the testicles and prostate gland in men, which may reduce fertility in a small number of cases
Rarely, spread through the bloodstream, which can cause sepsis
Premature birth in pregnancy, and a serious eye infection in a baby infected during birth, which can cause blindness if not treated with antibiotics

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of gonorrhoea?
sections.body:
Not everyone with gonorrhoea has symptoms, which is why testing matters if infection is possible. When symptoms appear, they usually start around two weeks after infection, although they sometimes do not appear until many months later.

In people with a penis, the most common signs are discharge from the tip of the penis, pain when peeing and sore testicles. In people with a vagina, signs include more vaginal discharge, pain in the lower abdomen, pain when peeing, and bleeding between periods or after sex. Infection of the throat usually causes no symptoms, while infection of the rectum or the eyes can cause discharge, pain or irritation.

Because symptoms can be mild or absent, a person can pass the infection on without knowing. The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111 for someone who has, or may have, gonorrhoea and has red, itchy or painful eyes, a high temperature, joint pain or swelling, or a spotty or blotchy rash.

sections.heading: How is gonorrhoea passed on?
sections.body:
Gonorrhoea is caused by a bacterium called Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It is passed on through vaginal, anal or oral sex without a condom. Sharing sex toys that have not been washed or covered with a new condom each time can also pass it on. A parent can pass the infection to a baby during birth, and the bacteria can sometimes pass from the genitals to the fingers and then to the eyes, where they may cause an eye infection.

The bacterium cannot survive outside the human body for long. NHS sources say that kissing, hugging, swimming pools, toilet seats and sharing towels, cups, plates or cutlery do not spread it. People without symptoms can still pass it on.

Having had gonorrhoea before does not give lasting protection, so it can be caught again. UKHSA data show that around half of gonorrhoea diagnoses in England in 2024 were in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men. UKHSA also reported fewer gonorrhoea diagnoses in England in 2024 than in 2023, though the fall was smaller in this group of men than overall.

sections.heading: How is gonorrhoea diagnosed?
sections.body:
Testing uses a urine sample or a swab. A person can be tested even when they have no symptoms. The NHS lists sexual health clinics and GP surgeries as places that test for gonorrhoea, and some pharmacies and online services also offer testing. Some services provide a free self-test kit, although home tests can vary in accuracy, and NHS 111 Wales advises using a local sexual health service.

NHS 111 Wales lists testing as sensible after symptoms, after sex with a new partner without a condom, after a partner is diagnosed with an STI, and when pregnant or planning a pregnancy. Some clinics can give rapid results. After recent sex, a person may be advised to wait up to a week to be tested, or to repeat the test two weeks later.

Treatment can start before the test results arrive when infection is likely. Current and recent sexual partners need testing too. Clinic leaflets describe telling partners from roughly the last six months, and a sexual health clinic can contact them anonymously for the person if they wish. Treatment at sexual health clinics is free.

sections.heading: How is gonorrhoea treated?
sections.body:
Gonorrhoea is treated with antibiotics. In most cases this is a single antibiotic injection, given in the buttock or thigh. Sometimes a tablet can be used instead of an injection, if the person prefers. Treatment can start before the test results arrive.

The NHS asks people to return to the GP surgery or sexual health clinic about a week after starting treatment to be tested again, while other services describe a follow-up after about two weeks. BASHH's 2025 guideline says a routine test of cure is not necessary for infections of the genitals or anus treated with ceftriaxone when the infection is susceptible to it. It still recommends one for some people, including those with persistent symptoms, a throat infection, an unknown susceptibility or pregnancy, so follow-up advice can differ.

The NHS advises no vaginal, anal or oral sex until the person and any partner have completed treatment and tests show the infection has gone. The BASHH leaflet advises waiting until seven days after both the person and their partners have taken treatment, and that this includes sex with a condom.

Reinfection is possible, because earlier treatment does not give immunity. Some strains of gonorrhoea are becoming resistant to antibiotics. The UKHSA GRASP report says that most ceftriaxone-resistant cases continue to be associated with travel to the Asia-Pacific region.

sections.heading: What problems can untreated gonorrhoea cause?
sections.body:
If gonorrhoea is treated early, it is unlikely to cause lasting problems. Left untreated, it can spread and cause serious harm. The NHS says the more times a person has gonorrhoea, the more likely complications become.

In women, the infection can reach the reproductive organs and cause pelvic inflammatory disease. This can lead to long-term pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy and infertility. In men, it can cause a painful infection of the testicles and prostate gland, which may reduce fertility in a small number of cases.

In rare cases the infection spreads through the bloodstream to other parts of the body, which can cause life-threatening infection (sepsis). The UKHSA Green Book describes this wider spread as disseminated gonococcal infection.

In pregnancy, gonorrhoea can increase the risk of premature birth, a low birth weight baby and miscarriage. The infection can also pass to the baby during birth, and it can cause blindness if it is not treated with antibiotics. Babies at risk are usually given antibiotics straight after birth. For this reason the NHS says treatment during pregnancy is important.

sections.heading: Can gonorrhoea be prevented?
sections.body:
The NHS recommends condoms for vaginal and anal sex, and a condom or a latex or plastic dam for oral sex. Testing once a year, and when there is a new sexual partner, is also recommended.

There is currently no licensed vaccine against the gonorrhoea bacterium itself, according to the UKHSA Green Book. Developing one has been difficult.

In England, the 4CMenB vaccine, which is licensed for meningococcal group B disease, began to be offered for gonorrhoea prevention on 1 August 2025. It is offered mainly to gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men who are at higher risk of gonorrhoea, through specialist sexual health services. Protection against gonorrhoea is not a licensed use of the vaccine, so this use is off-label.

UKHSA guidance describes the protection as partial, with studies reporting roughly 30 to 40% protection, and says the vaccine is not complete protection, so condoms remain important. The main benefit is expected across the community rather than for each person.

faqs.a: Gonorrhoea is treated with antibiotics, most often a single injection, and sometimes a tablet can be used instead. The NHS asks people to return about a week after starting treatment to be tested again. Having had gonorrhoea does not give lasting protection, so it can be caught again. Some strains of gonorrhoea are becoming resistant to antibiotics.

faqs.a: Not everyone with gonorrhoea has symptoms, and a person without symptoms can still pass it on. A person can be tested even when they have no symptoms. Testing is available at sexual health clinics and GP surgeries, and some pharmacies and online services also offer it. Infection of the throat usually causes no symptoms.

faqs.q: Does gonorrhoea cause infertility?
faqs.a: Infertility is a possible complication of gonorrhoea that is not treated. The NHS says that if it is treated early, lasting problems are unlikely. In women, spread to the reproductive organs can cause pelvic inflammatory disease, which can lead to infertility. In men, a painful infection of the testicles and prostate may reduce fertility in a small number of cases.

faqs.q: Can gonorrhoea affect pregnancy?
faqs.a: Gonorrhoea in pregnancy can increase the risk of premature birth, a low birth weight baby and miscarriage. It can also pass to the baby during birth and cause blindness if not treated with antibiotics. NHS inform advises anyone who is pregnant and thinks they have gonorrhoea to contact their GP practice or midwife.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for gonorrhoea?
faqs.a: There is currently no licensed vaccine against the gonorrhoea bacterium itself. Since August 2025, England has offered the 4CMenB vaccine, an off-label use, to some people at higher risk, mainly gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men. UKHSA guidance describes the protection as partial rather than complete, so condoms remain important.

sections.heading: What is genital herpes and what are the symptoms?
sections.body:
Genital herpes is an infection of the genital area caused by the herpes simplex virus. NHS inform says most people with the virus do not notice any symptoms and do not know they have it. Carrying the virus without symptoms is not a sign that anyone has done something wrong. One UK sexual health service notes that some people do not get symptoms until months or sometimes years after catching the virus.

When symptoms do appear, the same service says they usually start between two and twelve days after contact with the virus, although sources differ. A first episode can begin with red skin and bumps that change into blisters, and fever, body aches or swollen glands may also occur. The blisters burst and leave painful red sores. The World Health Organization says symptoms often begin with tingling, itching or burning near where the sores will appear.

NHS sexual health information describes a first episode as lasting two to four weeks. Symptoms clear up on their own but can come back. Repeat episodes are generally less severe and clear up more quickly than the first, and some people never have another outbreak.

sections.heading: How does the virus spread?
sections.body:
Genital herpes is passed on through sex. The NHS advises avoiding vaginal, anal and oral sex until the sores have gone away. It says the virus can spread from the first tingling of an outbreak until the sores have fully healed, and that it may also be passed on when there are no symptoms.

Two types of the virus cause genital herpes. GOV.UK says HSV-1 mainly causes cold sores but can also cause genital infection. The 2024 BASHH guideline describes HSV-1 as now the most common cause of genital herpes in the UK, while HSV-2 is more likely to cause recurrent anogenital symptoms.

Condoms lower the risk of passing the virus on but do not remove it entirely, according to the NHS. Herpes can still be passed on if the condom does not cover the infected area. Because most people with genital herpes have no symptoms or only very mild ones, the virus can be passed on by people who do not know they carry it.

sections.heading: How is genital herpes diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says a sexual health clinic can test for genital herpes by taking fluid from a blister or sore with a small swab. The swab may be uncomfortable for a moment. The test cannot be done if there are no visible blisters or sores. One sexual health service notes that a sore that has become too dry may be less likely to give a positive result.

The NHS advises visiting a sexual health clinic if there are symptoms, and many clinics offer a walk-in service, so an appointment may not be needed. A GP can also be seen, but will probably refer to a sexual health clinic if genital herpes is suspected.

NHS inform advises booking an appointment with the local sexual health service for free testing.

sections.heading: What treatments and self-care are available?
sections.body:
There is no cure for genital herpes. For a first episode, the NHS says antiviral medicine is prescribed and works best if started within 5 days of symptoms appearing, and cream may be offered for the pain. Outbreaks often clear up by themselves. The NHS says some people who have frequent outbreaks may benefit from taking antiviral medicine every day for several months.

US CDC guidance says suppressive antiviral treatment reduces how often genital herpes recurs in people who have frequent recurrences, and that quality of life is improved for many of them. The CDC says suppression for HSV-1 should be reserved for those with frequent recurrences. It adds that suppressive treatment, taken consistently and correctly, can reduce but not eliminate the risk of passing the virus on.

Self-care described by the NHS includes keeping the area clean with plain or salt water and using an ice pack wrapped in a flannel. Petroleum jelly or lidocaine cream may be used, and passing urine while pouring water over the genitals can ease the pain.

sections.heading: Genital herpes in pregnancy
sections.body:
The main concern in pregnancy is neonatal herpes, a serious illness in a newborn baby. The NHS says it can be fatal, but most babies recover with treatment. The risk of passing the virus on during a vaginal birth is higher if genital herpes is caught for the first time in the last 6 weeks of pregnancy, and is much lower for people who have had genital herpes before or who catch it in early pregnancy.

The NHS says antiviral medicine is offered from around 32 weeks of pregnancy to reduce this risk. A BASHH patient leaflet describes antiviral tablets from 32 weeks until the baby is born for a first episode late in pregnancy. Some local NHS trust leaflets give different schedules, so the plan is agreed with the midwife or doctor.

BASHH algorithms recommend a planned caesarean especially if a first episode occurs within 6 weeks of delivery. A joint BASHH and Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists guideline on herpes in pregnancy and the newborn was updated in 2024. The NHS advises telling a midwife or doctor about a history of genital herpes, or if symptoms are suspected during pregnancy.

sections.heading: Living with genital herpes
sections.body:
MedlinePlus (US) says outbreaks become less frequent over time, and the CDC says the number of outbreaks tends to fall over a period of years even though the virus stays in the body. The pattern varies widely, with some people having only one outbreak or only rare ones.

MedlinePlus lists reasons to contact a healthcare provider: outbreaks that worsen despite medicine and self-care, severe pain, sores that do not heal, frequent outbreaks, and outbreaks during pregnancy. It also advises contact if fever, headache or vomiting develop during or after an outbreak. In the UK, the NHS names a sexual health clinic or a GP as the places to go with genital herpes symptoms.

The 2024 BASHH guideline covers diagnostic tests, first episodes and recurrences, treatment, preventing transmission between partners and patient-centred counselling.

faqs.q: Can genital herpes be cured?
faqs.a: There is no cure for genital herpes, according to the NHS. Symptoms clear up on their own but can come back, and antiviral medicine can be used. The NHS says some people who have frequent outbreaks may benefit from taking antiviral medicine for several months. Self-care measures such as keeping the area clean with plain or salt water can also help.

faqs.q: Can the virus be passed on without sores?
faqs.a: Yes, the NHS says genital herpes may be passed on even when there are no symptoms. It can spread from the first tingling of an outbreak until the sores have fully healed. Condoms lower the risk but do not remove it entirely, and herpes can still be passed on if the condom does not cover the infected area.

faqs.a: One of the two viruses involved, HSV-1, is the usual cause of cold sores, and GOV.UK says it can also cause genital infection. The 2024 BASHH guideline describes HSV-1 as now the most common cause of genital herpes in the UK. HSV-2 is more likely to cause recurrent anogenital symptoms.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of pre-eclampsia?
sections.body:
The NHS says pre-eclampsia often has no noticeable symptoms, and that its early signs, high blood pressure and protein in the urine, are usually found at routine antenatal appointments. Tommy's says these signs usually appear after 20 weeks of pregnancy, although pre-eclampsia can start earlier or soon after delivery. NHS inform lists blood pressure rising in mid or late pregnancy, and a baby who is not growing well, as key indicators.

Later symptoms listed by the NHS include a severe headache that simple painkillers do not ease, vision problems such as blurring or flashing lights, pain just below the ribs, vomiting, heartburn that does not settle with heartburn medicines, feeling very unwell, and sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet. Tommy's notes that swollen hands and feet are common in late pregnancy but can also be a sign of pre-eclampsia.

sections.heading: When should urgent help be sought?
sections.body:
The NHS says anyone who is pregnant, or who has given birth in the last few weeks, and has symptoms of pre-eclampsia should get urgent medical help. A pregnant person is advised to call the maternity unit if they have the number. Someone who has recently given birth, or who cannot reach the maternity unit, is advised to call NHS 111. The NHS symptoms page also says to get medical advice immediately by calling the GP surgery or NHS 111.

For a life-threatening emergency at any stage of pregnancy, the NHS says to call 999. NHS inform advises contacting a midwife or GP immediately for very swollen ankles, fingers, hands or face. Severe pre-eclampsia can progress to seizures, called eclampsia, which need emergency care. The NHS says pre-eclampsia usually improves soon after the birth, but complications can sometimes develop a few days later, so the same symptoms still matter after delivery.

sections.heading: What causes pre-eclampsia and who is more likely to get it?
sections.body:
The NHS says the cause of pre-eclampsia is not fully understood. It is thought to happen when there is a problem with the placenta, the organ that connects the pregnancy to the pregnant person's blood supply and feeds the baby.

Risk factors listed by the NHS include a first pregnancy, more than ten years since the last pregnancy, a previous pregnancy with pre-eclampsia, and a close family member, such as a mother or sister, who had it. Diabetes, high blood pressure and kidney disease are also listed. NHS inform adds being overweight or obese before pregnancy. Local NHS trust guidance also lists older age and a multiple pregnancy, such as twins, and a research review includes autoimmune disorders among the risk factors. Having a risk factor does not mean pre-eclampsia will develop.

sections.heading: How is pre-eclampsia diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says pre-eclampsia is usually found through blood pressure and urine checks at routine antenatal appointments. If doctors think it may be present, they may offer a blood test that measures a protein called placental growth factor, or PlGF, to help rule it out during part of pregnancy. The NHS says that if PlGF levels are high, it is highly likely that the person does not have pre-eclampsia. If levels are low, it could be a sign of pre-eclampsia, but further tests are needed to confirm the diagnosis.

A Scottish health technologies group says the PlGF-based test can help clinicians make a diagnosis when used alongside standard clinical assessment. It adds that the test does not show how severe the condition is, and that its results should not be used to make decisions about the timing of birth in preterm pre-eclampsia.

sections.heading: How is pre-eclampsia treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says the only way to cure pre-eclampsia is to deliver the baby, so the person is usually monitored regularly until delivery is possible. This is normally close to full term, but it may be earlier in more severe cases. Delivery can be induced or done by caesarean section, and blood pressure medicine is offered while waiting. NHS inform says moderate or severe cases may mean an earlier delivery.

The NHS says medicines for high blood pressure reduce the likelihood of serious complications, such as stroke. NHS trust guidance says blood pressure medicine can be given as tablets or through a drip. People diagnosed earlier in pregnancy may need to be admitted to hospital for blood pressure treatment and monitoring for complications while the birth is planned. Trial summaries describe magnesium sulfate as the standard medicine used to prevent and treat seizures in severe pre-eclampsia.

sections.heading: What complications can it cause, and can it be prevented?
sections.body:
NHS inform says pre-eclampsia can affect the liver, lungs, kidneys, brain, blood-clotting system and heart, and that moderate or severe cases may need an earlier delivery. A baby may not grow as well as expected, and an NHS trust leaflet notes that the baby may be smaller and may need to be born early. The NHS names stroke as a serious complication that blood pressure medicine helps to reduce.

The NHS says pre-eclampsia cannot be prevented, but people at high risk may be advised to take low-dose aspirin during pregnancy. NHS trust leaflets say aspirin will not prevent every case, and Tommy's says there is good evidence that it slightly reduces the risk. Trust guidance based on NICE guidance recommends it for people with one or more high-risk factors, or with more than one moderate risk factor.

sections.heading: What happens after the birth and what is the outlook?
sections.body:
Action on Pre-eclampsia says pre-eclampsia always goes away eventually after the baby is born, which may happen within hours or take up to six months. Blood pressure typically falls straight after birth and then rises to a peak a few days later. After discharge, blood pressure is measured regularly by the community midwife or GP until the high blood pressure has resolved, and medication is reduced gradually. If high blood pressure persists after the birth, the charity says it is diagnosed as non-pregnancy hypertension, which needs treatment to control cardiovascular problems in later life.

Tommy's says giving birth resolves the symptoms in most cases, although in a small number they continue. NHS inform says women who have had pre-eclampsia have a higher risk of high blood pressure, stroke or heart disease later in life.

faqs.q: Can pre-eclampsia be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says the only way to cure pre-eclampsia is to deliver the baby. Until delivery is possible, the person is usually monitored regularly, and blood pressure medicine is offered while waiting. Action on Pre-eclampsia says the condition always goes away eventually after the birth, which may happen within hours or take up to six months.

faqs.q: Can pre-eclampsia happen after the baby is born?
faqs.a: Tommy's says pre-eclampsia can start soon after delivery, and the NHS says complications can develop a few days after the birth. Action on Pre-eclampsia says women should be told which symptoms to look out for and who to contact if unwell. The NHS says anyone who has recently given birth and has symptoms is advised to call NHS 111.

faqs.q: Who is more likely to get pre-eclampsia?
faqs.a: The NHS lists a first pregnancy, more than ten years since the last pregnancy, a previous pregnancy with pre-eclampsia, a close family member who had it, diabetes, high blood pressure and kidney disease. NHS inform adds being overweight or obese before pregnancy. Having a risk factor is not a diagnosis, and the condition is found through antenatal checks.

faqs.q: Who should be contacted if symptoms of pre-eclampsia appear?
faqs.a: The NHS says symptoms of pre-eclampsia in someone who is pregnant, or who has given birth in the last few weeks, need urgent medical help. A pregnant person is advised to call the maternity unit if they have the number. NHS 111 is the route after a recent birth or if the unit cannot be reached, and the NHS says to call 999 for a life-threatening emergency.

faqs.q: Is existing high blood pressure linked to pre-eclampsia?
faqs.a: The NHS lists existing high blood pressure as a risk factor for pre-eclampsia, alongside diabetes and kidney disease. People at high risk may be advised to take low-dose aspirin during pregnancy, and the NHS says pre-eclampsia cannot be prevented. NHS trust leaflets say aspirin does not prevent every case of pre-eclampsia.

faqs.q: Does pre-eclampsia affect health later in life?
faqs.a: NHS inform says women who have had pre-eclampsia have a higher risk of high blood pressure, stroke or heart disease later in life. Action on Pre-eclampsia says that if high blood pressure persists after the birth, it is diagnosed as non-pregnancy hypertension, which needs treatment to control cardiovascular problems in later life.

gestational-diabetes.name: Gestational diabetes
gestational-diabetes.definition: Gestational diabetes is a form of diabetes that starts during pregnancy and typically clears up after the baby is born.
gestational-diabetes.overview: Gestational diabetes is a form of diabetes that starts during pregnancy in women who did not have diabetes before. Hormones made during pregnancy can make insulin less effective, and some women cannot make enough insulin to overcome this. Most people have no symptoms, so it is usually found through screening with a blood test. Care starts with changes to diet and physical activity, and medicine is added if blood sugar stays too high. It typically clears up after the birth, but it raises the chance of type 2 diabetes later.
causes: Hormones made during pregnancy can make the body's cells respond poorly to insulin, which is called insulin resistance.
Most women make enough extra insulin to compensate, but some cannot, and they develop gestational diabetes.
riskFactors: A higher body mass index (BMI), which the NHS lists among the factors that raise the chance.
Having had gestational diabetes in an earlier pregnancy.
Having had a previous baby who was large at birth.
A parent or sibling with diabetes.
A South Asian, Black, African-Caribbean or Middle Eastern family background.
Being over 40.
signs: Raised blood sugar found on a screening blood test, often in someone who feels well.
A baby who is growing larger than usual.
complications: For the baby: excess growth, birth injury, low blood sugar and jaundice after birth, and, rarely, stillbirth.
For the mother: pre-eclampsia, premature labour and too much amniotic fluid.
A higher chance of type 2 diabetes later in life.
A higher chance of gestational diabetes in future pregnancies.
gestational-diabetes.diagnosis: The midwife or doctor asks questions at the booking appointment to work out whether someone is at increased risk. Screening usually uses a blood test called an oral glucose tolerance test, which takes about two hours, and the NHS says it is done between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. Women who have had gestational diabetes before are offered testing early in pregnancy. Timing and thresholds differ between UK nations and local services.
gestational-diabetes.treatment: Treatment starts with changes to diet and physical activity. Medicine may be added if blood sugar is still not stable 1 to 2 weeks after those changes, or if it is very high at diagnosis. The options are tablets, usually metformin, or insulin injections. Insulin is usually offered if metformin does not work well enough or causes side effects. Medicines are usually stopped after the birth. During labour, blood sugar is monitored and kept under control, and a glucose and insulin drip may be needed.
gestational-diabetes.prevention: NHS hospital leaflets suggest that being physically active, keeping to a healthy weight and eating a healthy balanced diet after the birth can lower the chance of type 2 diabetes after gestational diabetes. Diabetes UK says gestational diabetes is not directly caused by sugar, but overweight or obesity raises the risk.
gestational-diabetes.seekCare: NHS inform notes that some symptoms of high blood sugar are also normal in pregnancy, and most cases are found through screening blood tests rather than symptoms. Anyone concerned about their blood sugar or their pregnancy can contact their GP, midwife or maternity unit. Maternity services advise contacting the midwife or maternity unit straight away if a baby's movements slow, weaken or stop. After the birth, a blood test to check for diabetes is recommended, with a yearly test if the result is normal. Call 999 in an emergency.

sections.heading: What is gestational diabetes and why does it happen?
sections.body:
Gestational diabetes is a form of diabetes that starts during pregnancy. Diabetes UK describes it as affecting women who did not have diabetes before, and it typically clears up after the baby is born. Insulin is the hormone that helps the body handle sugar in the blood. Pregnancy brings hormones and other changes that make the body's cells respond poorly to insulin. NIDDK explains that most women compensate, but some cannot make enough insulin to overcome this resistance, and they develop gestational diabetes.

Some people are more likely to develop it than others. The NHS lists a higher BMI, having had gestational diabetes before, a previous large baby, a parent or sibling with diabetes, being over 40, and a South Asian, Black, African-Caribbean or Middle Eastern family background. Diabetes UK says gestational diabetes is not directly caused by sugar, but overweight or obesity raises the risk.

Diabetes UK says most women with gestational diabetes go on to have a healthy baby and a normal pregnancy, although it can cause serious health problems for the mother and baby if it is left untreated. The NHS says the risks can be reduced if the condition is found early and well managed.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms?
sections.body:
Most people with gestational diabetes have no symptoms. The NHS says most cases are found when blood sugar is tested during screening in pregnancy, and NIDDK also says it usually causes no symptoms.

Diabetes UK lists the signs that some women notice: going to the toilet to pass urine a lot, especially at night, being very thirsty, feeling more tired than usual, genital itching or thrush, and blurred eyesight. NHS inform also lists a dry mouth, and notes that some of these symptoms are normal in pregnancy. For that reason they cannot show on their own whether someone has gestational diabetes.

Because symptoms are often absent or hard to tell apart from pregnancy itself, the usual route to diagnosis is a blood test. Diabetes UK says most cases are found through a blood test during pregnancy. The next section describes how screening works.

sections.heading: How is gestational diabetes found?
sections.body:
Risk is assessed at the booking appointment, which the NHS places at around 8 to 12 weeks of pregnancy. The midwife or doctor asks questions to work out whether someone is at increased risk.

The usual test is an oral glucose tolerance test, a blood test that takes about two hours according to NHS inform. The NHS and Diabetes UK say it is done between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. NHS inform describes a slightly different pattern for Scotland, where people with risk factors are offered an HbA1c blood test first and a screening test at around 24 weeks.

NICE says women who have had gestational diabetes before should be tested as soon as possible, and that testing is also offered to women with a previous history who book in the second trimester. NICE says other women with risk factors are offered a two-hour glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks. Timing and thresholds vary between UK nations and local services, so the maternity team explains the arrangements that apply.

sections.heading: How is it treated?
sections.body:
Treatment starts with changes to diet and physical activity. The NHS treatment page describes physical activity as a way to lower blood sugar, and Diabetes UK also lists diet and exercise as the first step.

Medicine may be offered if blood sugar is still not stable 1 to 2 weeks after those changes, or if it is very high at diagnosis. The options are tablets, usually metformin, or insulin injections. The NHS says insulin is usually offered if metformin does not work well enough, causes side effects, or blood sugar is very high. Most people who use insulin take a rapid-acting type before meals, sometimes with a longer-acting type once a day, and the NHS says insulin needs often rise as pregnancy goes on.

NHS maternity services advise giving birth in hospital. The NHS says blood sugar is monitored and kept under control during labour and birth, and a glucose and insulin drip may be needed. Diabetes UK says delivery may need to be earlier if there are complications such as high blood pressure or a larger-than-average baby.

sections.heading: What happens after the birth?
sections.body:
NICE says blood glucose-lowering medicine for gestational diabetes should be stopped straight after the birth. NHS hospital guides say blood sugar is usually checked for a day or two after delivery.

The NHS and Diabetes UK recommend a blood test to check for diabetes 6 to 13 weeks after the birth. NICE describes this as a fasting plasma glucose test. Diabetes UK explains that a small number of women continue to have raised blood sugar after pregnancy, which is why the test matters.

If the result is normal, Diabetes UK and NICE advise a test once a year, because having had gestational diabetes raises the chance of type 2 diabetes later in life. NICE advises a yearly HbA1c test for women whose postnatal test showed no diabetes. NHS hospital leaflets say gestational diabetes is likely to come back in a future pregnancy, and many trusts arrange an early glucose test in the next one. The maternity team or GP can explain the local arrangements.

sections.heading: How can it affect the baby and the mother?
sections.body:
The NHS says gestational diabetes can affect the baby, although most babies are healthy. Extra sugar in the mother's blood can make the baby grow larger than usual, which NHS inform links to difficulties during birth and a higher likelihood of induced labour or a caesarean section. Diabetes UK also links a larger baby to a more difficult birth, and lists jaundice, which is yellowing of the skin and eyes, after birth.

NHS hospital guides say a baby may have low blood sugar after birth, so the baby's blood sugar is checked, and if it is low the baby may need temporary feeding through a tube or drip. The NHS overview lists loss of the baby as a possible complication, but a rare one.

For the mother, NHS hospital guides list pre-eclampsia, a condition that affects blood pressure in pregnancy, and NHS inform links too much amniotic fluid to premature labour. Good blood sugar control reduces these risks.

faqs.q: Does gestational diabetes go away after the baby is born?
faqs.a: Diabetes UK and NHS sources say it typically clears up after the birth, and NICE says glucose-lowering medicine is stopped straight afterwards. A blood test to check for diabetes is recommended 6 to 13 weeks after the birth, because a small number of women continue to have raised blood sugar after pregnancy.

faqs.q: Can gestational diabetes affect the baby?
faqs.a: Possible effects for the baby include excess growth, a more difficult birth, low blood sugar and jaundice after birth, and, rarely, stillbirth. Diabetes UK says most women with gestational diabetes go on to have a healthy baby, and the NHS says the risks can be reduced if the condition is found early and well managed.

faqs.q: Does it mean I will develop type 2 diabetes?
faqs.a: Having had gestational diabetes raises the chance of developing type 2 diabetes, but the sources do not say it will happen. Diabetes UK and NICE advise a blood test once a year after a normal result. NHS hospital leaflets suggest being active, keeping to a healthy weight and eating a balanced diet to lower the risk.

faqs.q: Is gestational diabetes treated with tablets or insulin?
faqs.a: Diet and physical activity come first. If blood sugar stays too high, the usual medicine is metformin tablets, and insulin injections are the other option. The NHS says insulin is usually offered if metformin does not work well enough, causes side effects, or blood sugar is very high. The clinician decides which is suitable.

faqs.q: Can it happen again in another pregnancy?
faqs.a: NHS hospital leaflets say gestational diabetes is likely to come back in a future pregnancy, and many trusts arrange an early glucose test in the next one. NICE says women who have had it before should be tested as soon as possible in a new pregnancy. The midwife or GP explains the local arrangements.

miscarriage.name: Miscarriage
miscarriage.overview: A miscarriage is the loss of a pregnancy. Vaginal bleeding is the main sign, ranging from light spotting to heavy bleeding, and lower tummy cramping and pain are also typical. Some people have no symptoms and learn of the loss at a scan, which is called a missed miscarriage. The NHS says the cause is often not identified, and that it may take some time to recover physically and emotionally. Tommy's says miscarriages are very rarely caused by something the person did or did not do.
causes: In the first trimester, a miscarriage is usually linked to problems with the unborn baby, according to the NHS.
Chromosome problems are the most common cause of early miscarriage, and Tommy's says these happen by chance.
For later miscarriages the NHS lists long-term conditions, infections and a weakened cervix.
The NHS says the cause of some miscarriages is often not identified.
riskFactors: NHS inform Scotland lists smoking and heavy caffeine or alcohol use as raising the risk of miscarriage without directly causing it.
Tommy's lists a body mass index outside the healthy range, heavy drinking and poorly managed diabetes as possible contributors.
The NHS lists poorly controlled diabetes and thyroid disorders as long-term conditions that can raise the risk of a later miscarriage.
Tommy's says the risk of miscarriage increases as the biological parents get older.
signs: Vaginal bleeding, from light spotting to heavy bleeding.
No symptoms at all in a missed miscarriage, found at a scan.
complications: Heavy bleeding that soaks a pad, which the NHS lists as a reason to call 999.
A high temperature (fever), which NHS inform Scotland lists as a reason to seek medical advice immediately.
Emotional effects, with the NHS noting that recovery can take some time physically and emotionally.
miscarriage.diagnosis: NICE says people referred with suspected miscarriage are offered an ultrasound scan to identify where the pregnancy is and whether it is viable. Where the scan and the date of the last period disagree, NICE says the scan findings guide management. Some people have no symptoms and learn of a missed miscarriage at a scan.
miscarriage.treatment: NHS inform Scotland describes three ways to manage a miscarriage: waiting for it to finish on its own, tablets (medical management), or an operation to remove the pregnancy from the womb. NICE says clinicians should discuss all the options so that the person can make an informed choice.
miscarriage.prevention: The NHS says an increased risk of miscarriage is not linked to emotional stress, shock, exercise, lifting, working, sex, air travel or spicy food. Tommy's has a page on reducing the risk of miscarriage and lists body mass index outside a healthy range, heavy drinking, air pollution and poorly managed diabetes as possible contributors.
miscarriage.seekCare: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for heavy red bleeding that soaks a pad, severe tummy pain, shoulder pain, or feeling faint or losing consciousness. NHS inform Scotland says that before 12 weeks the advice is to contact the GP practice or local early pregnancy unit, or phone 111 if the GP practice is closed. From 12 weeks it advises contacting the local maternity service. It also advises seeking medical advice straight away for a high temperature or for pain that pain relief does not control.
